title: Fermi gas of polar molecules in the Pauli-blocked regime
authors: Junyu Lin, Annette N. Carroll, Phillip Martin, Calder Miller, Reuben R. W. Wang, Kevin Xu, John L. Bohn, Tim de Jongh, Jun Ye
abstract: Quantum gases of polar molecules have recently emerged as a powerful platform for exploring exotic many-body dynamics and correlated quantum behavior. To achieve the full potential of this platform, the production of deeply degenerate quantum gases of molecules in arbitrary confinement geometries is necessary. Here, we successfully evaporate fermionic KRb molecules in both 3D and quasi-2D geometries to well below their Fermi temperatures utilizing dipolar collisions. As we evaporate deeper into degeneracy in both geometries, we enter the Pauli-blocked regime with polar molecules, which we independently confirm for the first time by measuring the Pauli suppression of elastic collisions. Moreover, the Pauli suppression of collisions contributes to the limitation of our final molecular temperature to about 25% of the Fermi temperature in both geometries, particularly limiting quasi-2D evaporation where the Pauli blockade drastically reduces an otherwise large elastic to inelastic scattering ratio. This work demonstrates the production of degenerate Fermi gases of polar molecules both in a 3D harmonic trap and in mono- and bi-layer 2D configurations. Further, our work explores the fundamental limits on evaporation of molecular Fermi gases set by the Pauli-exclusion principle, which could be overcome in the future by introducing distinguishable scattering partners.
summary: The study reports on achieving deep degeneracy in fermionic polar molecular gases in both 3D and quasi-2D traps. By measuring density fluctuations and analyzing collision rates, the authors confirm that the Pauli exclusion principle imposes a fundamental limit on how cold these quantum systems can be cooled. This work is crucial for designing future experiments aiming to explore exotic many-body physics beyond simple thermal equilibrium.
main_problem: The study investigates achieving deep degeneracy in quantum gases of polar molecules while quantifying the fundamental limitations imposed by the Pauli exclusion principle during evaporative cooling.
main_result: The authors successfully produced degenerate Fermi gases in both 3D and quasi-2D geometries, confirming that Pauli blockade significantly limits the lowest achievable temperatures, especially in lower dimensions.
method: The research combines experimental measurements of density fluctuations and cross sections with advanced theoretical modeling (Monte Carlo simulations and solving radial Schrödinger equations) to quantify these quantum statistical effects.
model_or_system: The system is a Fermi gas of fermionic polar molecules ($	ext{KRb}$) trapped in harmonic or quasi-2D optical potentials. Interactions are dominated by engineered repulsive dipole-dipole collisions, allowing for precise control over scattering cross sections.
key_observables: Reduced temperature ($T/T_F$), Pauli suppression factor ($\eta$), elastic and inelastic collision cross sections ($\sigma_{el}, \sigma_{in}$), and density fluctuations ($	ext{Var } N/N_{	ext{;}}$).
important_parameters: The primary limiting factors are the Pauli exclusion principle, which restricts scattering rates, and one-body heating from the trap potential.
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include using the Local Density Approximation (LDA) for thermometry and assuming adiabaticity during electric field ramping for cooling analysis.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate evaporative cooling trajectories ($T$ vs $N$, $T/T_F$ vs $N$) comparing experimental data to simulations incorporating Pauli suppression. Other figures detail density fluctuation measurements and the temperature dependence of cross sections derived from thermalization rate analyses.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the platform (polar molecules in 3D/2D), then detailing multiple diagnostic techniques (density fluctuations, CDT) to measure degeneracy and interaction rates. The core argument builds by comparing cooling trajectories across dimensions, culminating in a quantitative assessment of Pauli blockade as the ultimate limit.
why_interesting: This work provides crucial experimental benchmarks for understanding how quantum statistics constrain evaporative cooling in dipolar systems, which is vital for realizing highly correlated quantum phases like superfluidity or novel magnetic states.
